title: Seven days of silence (Job 2:11–13)
hook: his friends sit with him for a week without speaking; that's the best thing they do

segments.voice: Yesterday, Job in the ashes, still blessing God's name. Your line was the Lord gave, the Lord took. What did you handle gently? Day four hundred forty-three.

The funeral home. The hospital corridor. The kitchen of a friend whose marriage just ended. Someone walks in with a casserole or a card, mind racing for the right thing to say. Everything sounds wrong. They're in a better place. It'll get easier. Everything happens for a reason. A mouth opens, and closes again. The silence is hard to bear, and it is tempting to fill it with something. Three men in the book of Job, at least at first, did something braver. They said nothing at all. For a week.
screen: `THE HOSPITAL CORRIDOR.` → `RACING FOR THE RIGHT WORDS.` → `THREE MEN SAY NOTHING.`

segments.voice: The King James Bible: "Now when Job's three friends heard of all this evil that was come upon him, they came every one from his own place; Eliphaz the Temanite, and Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite: for they had made an appointment together to come to mourn with him and to comfort him." Notice that. They made an appointment. They coordinated, traveled from three different places, and arrived together, on purpose. Then they see him from a distance, and they don't recognize him. Disease and grief have changed him that much. So they weep aloud, tear their robes, and throw dust into the air over their heads, the signs of mourning. And then this: "So they sat down with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him: for they saw that his grief was very great." On the ground, in the ash, at his level. Seven days of mourning appears elsewhere in the Bible too: Joseph mourned his father Jacob for seven days. Jews still keep that week of sitting with mourners today, called shiva, from the Hebrew for seven. Then a quiet detail. The friends don't speak until Job speaks first. They follow his lead. And here's the sad part, which the next days will show: once they open their mouths, it goes badly. Some readers say the week of silence was the best comfort they gave. Paul's letter to the Romans puts the same instinct simply: "weep with them that weep."
screen: `THEY MADE AN APPOINTMENT` · `THEY DIDN'T RECOGNIZE HIM` · `ON THE GROUND, SEVEN DAYS` · `NOT ONE WORD` · then, large: `FOR THEY SAW THAT HIS GRIEF WAS VERY GREAT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with someone without fixing. If someone near you is hurting and you can be with them today, go, and let silence be allowed. For now, in this sit, picture them. Imagine sitting down beside them, on the floor if that's where they are. Notice the urge to say something helpful. Let it rise and fall without acting on it. Just be there, breathing near them. If you pray, you can hold them before God without words. If you don't, simply keep them company in your mind. The bell holds the time.
Seven days of silence. Job's three friends sit on the ground with him for a week, and not one of them speaks.
Your line: they sat with him. Today, when someone tells you something painful, resist the first helpful sentence. Stay quiet a moment longer, and let them lead. Day four hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: Christians practice a ministry of presence by visiting the sick and the grieving, staying at wakes and sitting with the dying; many pastors and hospital chaplains point to Job's friends' silent week as a model.

fork.setup: your friend has lost his children, his health and everything he owned. you've traveled to see him and you barely recognize him. what do you do?
options: sit on the ground beside him and say nothing.
tell him it could have been worse.
fork.reveal: "so they sat down with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him." some readers call it the best thing they did.

original.note: Hebrew: seven days. the root of shiva, the Jewish week of mourning.

trapdoor: what you thought: Job's friends are the bad guys of the story.
what it means: they came on purpose, wept, and sat in silence for a week. the trouble only starts when they talk.
what a scholar hears: Joseph also mourned seven days (Genesis 50:10), and Jews keep a week of mourning called shiva.

notes: Shiva from Hebrew sheva/shiv'ah (seven). Confirm the brief, neighborly mention of Jewish practice.
Genesis 50:10: Joseph 'made a mourning for his father seven days.' Confirm.
'Many readers have said the week of silence was the best comfort they gave' follows the index hook; not attributed to a specific commentator.
Original: שִׁבְעַת יָמִים (shiv'at yamim) is the phrase in Job 2:13. Confirm pointing.
